ranking: 1. Buy and hold a low-cost S&P 500 fund (VOO/IVV, or SPY; VOO/IVV add only +0.03-0.04 pp/yr). Never sell, keep adding new money, and plan to end the position by donating appreciated lots or holding to a step-up at death. This is the only choice that meets the user's 'good confidence' bar, because its excess is about zero by construction. In CA no challenger passes that bar under any way the position can end.

2. If the user insists on a bet: keep at least 75% in an S&P core that is never sold, plus a small leveraged-trend sleeve (r2_combos A1/A3 form). Drawdowns were at or below SPY's in every history, the step-up penalty was small because the core is never sold, and the expected excess is about +1.5-2 pp/yr (grid median). It still has holdout p 0.12-0.30, DSR <= 0.04, a ~21% bootstrap chance of trailing SPY at 20 years, and lag-1 removes its 1986+ significance. The site cannot run it as a single preset.

3. The website's 'Beat the S&P: 2x trend (CA)' preset, all-in (SSO when SPY is >3% above SMA175, IEF when >3% below, daily at the close). It has the highest backtested excess at survivable drawdown. On real SSO 2006-26 in CA: score +4.48, full +3.67, boot p 0.116 (bootstrap CI about -1.0 to +7.8 pp/yr), max DD -48% vs -55%, and a Sharpe of 0.67 vs SPY's 0.65, so the excess is leverage rather than skill. Its weaknesses: SMA175/3% was chosen after the fact (DSR 0.002-0.006), its excess since 2010 is about zero, its whipsaw years are deep, it depends on executing at the same close, and it loses its significance when the position ends in a step-up or a gift. The pre-registered twin (SMA200/3% + 60-day short-term deferral) is essentially tied and is not on the site.

Its expected edge is about zero: score +0.66, it fails item 2, DSR 0.009, the 1986-2026 twin is negative (full -0.19, p 0.54), and the lead comes from QQQ/XLK in the menu. The book freezes into 50-60% growth/tech with 81-87% unrealized gains, and a replayed 2000-02 tech bust loses -56% to -71% vs SPY's -47.5%. That is concentration risk with no expected pay for it.
5. The 3x leveraged trend (UPRO/IEF, SMA175 or SMA200). Rejected: -88% to -93% in 1929-35, a 17-24% chance of an 80%+ drawdown within 20 years, and a one-day lag gives -76% in 1987.
6. Everything else (unlevered SPY timing, TAA, seasonality, dip/VIX, macro/curve, factor switches, global, sector rotation, stock picking, harvesting structures). All fail after CA tax.

judge:2.expected_excess_after_ca_tax:
The pick: 0.00 to +0.04 pp/yr vs SPY, by construction (VOO/IVV's lower fees add +0.03-0.04). Under a step-up or donation ending, buy-and-hold also gains relative to every realizing strategy.

The best challenger, the website's 2x trend preset (all-in), honestly: about +0.5 to +2 pp/yr expected after CA tax, central about +1. A given 20-year outcome could plausibly fall anywhere from about -3 to +5 pp/yr. The chance of trailing SPY at 20 years is about 25% (strategy-level bootstrap) to 60% (market-path bootstrap with 1-3 months of trend persistence).

How the range was built:
- Headline (first start): +3.7 to +3.8 full excess (2000-26 engine; real SSO 2006-26).
- Averaged over start dates, that falls to +1.6 (2000-26) and +2.3 (1986-26) for the pre-registered pick.
- The 1930-85 holdout gives full +2.5 / score +3.3 (p 0.16), but it is not significant.
- A step-up or donation ending takes off another 0.7-1.1 pp/yr (p rises to 0.20-0.29; worst 10-year window -1.5 to -1.8).
- The post-2010 decades were +0.6 and -0.3.
- Financing costs more now than in the near-zero-rate SSO era. The synthetic was about 0.55 pp/yr too cheap when T-bills were above 2%.
- Multiple-testing shrinkage applies after ~14,000 configs (DSR 0.002-0.006).

For the never-sold core + 25% sleeve, the whole account gets about +0.3 to +0.6 pp/yr.
caveats: Buy-and-hold is chosen because it is the only option that meets the user's 'good confidence' standard, not because it is expected to outperform. The 2x trend rule had positive after-tax excess in every history tested (2000-26, 1986-26, 1930-85), so buy-and-hold may well trail it over the next 20 years. The choice trades an uncertain, fat-tailed premium for certainty of the benchmark.

Buy-and-hold still carries full equity risk: -55% in 2007-09 and -81% to -84% in 1929-32. None of this research removes that. It has to be handled by overall asset allocation and an emergency fund, not by this account's strategy.

The 2x trend edge comes from a few slow bear markets (1929-32, 1973-74, 2000-02, 2007-09). Ten-year after-tax excess was +0.6 pp/yr in the 2010s and -0.3 in 2020-26. Pre-tax it trailed SPY in 13 of 26 calendar years, by 15-24 pp in 2011, 2015, 2016, 2020 and 2022. For start dates 2010-23 the SMA175 baseline's to-the-end excess averaged -0.47 pp/yr and was negative in 47% of them. The 100% 10-year beat rate on real SSO comes from 41 heavily overlapping windows, most of which contain 2008.

Behavioural survivability is poor. In fast corrections it loses more than the index: 2022 -37% to -41% vs -24%; 2015-16 -38% vs -13%; 1998 -36% vs -19%; 2011 -30% vs -19%. It then often re-enters late. Investors tend to quit in exactly those years, which locks in the whipsaw losses and misses the slow-bear payoff, which is where all of the edge lives.

Tail risk is real. A single -20% day while invested takes about 40% of the account at that close (roughly 5-7% odds over 20 years). From a 1929 start it still fell -77% by 1932. On 1930-85 windows the max DD was -67% to -73%. In the market-path bootstrap its median max DD is -59% to -66% (SPY -43% to -49%), and the chance of an 80% drawdown within 20 years is 5-11%. A 2x daily-reset fund would be wiped out by a -50% index day.

Execution is fragile. The rule must trade at the same day's close with a market-on-close order, deciding at about 3:45 pm ET (12:45 pm PT) every trading day for decades. One day late in October 1987 turns the escape into a -59% drawdown (1986-2026 p 0.26). Weekly checks fail. Missed days from vacations, illness or broker outages are a real risk.

Leveraged-ETF mechanics: SSO is a swap-based daily-reset fund with about a 0.9% expense ratio, financing at T-bills plus a spread, and volatility drag. Its distributions are ordinary income (4-5% of value in 2006-07; such a year can cost about 2 pp). There is counterparty risk and a small risk the fund closes, which would force a sale. The real-SSO record, 2006-26, includes about 10 years of near-zero rates, which flatters the leverage premium compared with today's.
The IEF off-leg relied on the 1982-2020 bond bull market. With T-bills as the safe asset, p is 0.14-0.20. In 2022 stocks and Treasuries fell together.

Tax issues the engine understates for the trend rule: it pays tax as it goes ($411k paid on a $100k start, real SSO 2006-26, vs $0 for SPY), so it loses deferral. The engine uses flat 48.1%/28.1% rates, but lumpy realizations in a large account can reach CA's 10.3-11.3% brackets and the federal 20% long-term / 37% short-term brackets, which buy-and-hold never triggers. Under a step-up or donation ending, none of the 54 2x neighbourhood configs passes bar items 1-3 in any history.

The 2x preset's parameters were chosen after the fact. SMA175/3% is the best point in its neighbourhood. On real SSO, SMA200/4% scores +2.4 (p 0.21, worst 10-year window -1.37), and SMA200 vs SMA175 moves sub-samples by about 1.5 pp/yr. Parameter selection inside the 2x structure has no out-of-sample skill on 1930-85 (PBO 0.60-0.82).

The 'Beat the S&P (CA)' momentum preset should not be used as a core holding. Its lead depends on QQQ/XLK being in the menu and on the start date, 5-year windows starting in 2020-21 lost 2.8-4.8 pp/yr, and its book cannot be de-risked without a large tax bill.

Several round-2 agents (Section 1256 futures, CAPE, options overlays, final rotation test, other markets) had not reported when this was written, and the r2_gap5 HIFO report was still pending its verdict. The recommendation should change only if one of them passes the full bar on data not used to find it. Nothing reviewed so far did.

Outside the engine, buy-and-hold can be improved slightly: tax-loss harvesting by swapping to a similar but not substantially identical index fund in drawdowns (about +0.2 pp/yr from offsetting other gains and the $3k ordinary-income deduction), avoiding wash sales with dividend reinvestment and IRA purchases, and donating the lowest-basis lots.
judge:2.what_to_tell_the_user: After testing about 14,000 strategies, nothing beat simply buying and holding an S&P 500 fund after California taxes with the confidence you asked for. My recommendation is to buy a low-cost S&P 500 fund (VOO or IVV), keep adding to it, and never sell it. If you eventually give the shares to charity or leave them to heirs, the gains are never taxed, which makes buy-and-hold even harder to beat. The best challenger is the website's 'Beat the S&P: 2x trend (CA)' preset. It did come out ahead in every history tested, but nearly all of that came from sidestepping a few slow bear markets (the 1930s, 1973-74, 2000-02, 2008), and since 2010 it has added roughly nothing after tax. It also has to be traded at the closing price on the exact day the signal changes, for decades: acting one day late in October 1987 turned a clean escape into a 59% loss. In fast sell-offs it loses more than the market, for example about -40% in 2022 when the S&P fell about 24%. A single 20%-down day while it is invested would take about 40% of the account at once. A realistic expectation is perhaps +0.5 to +2 percentage points a year after tax, with roughly a 1-in-4 to 1-in-2 chance of being behind the S&P after 20 years. The older 'Beat the S&P (CA)' momentum preset has an expected edge near zero and slowly turns into a concentrated tech bet you can't unwind without a big tax bill. If you still want the leveraged bet, keep it to a small side portion (20-25% at most) next to an S&P core you never sell. Follow its rules exactly, and decide in advance that you will stick with it through years when it trails by 15-20 points.
judge:2.reasoning:
This judgment looks at the downside. The question is whether any candidate earns a positive expected excess with 'good confidence', meaning it survives realistic endings, execution slips, tails and the investor's own behaviour. None does.

(1) Statistics. Every leveraged candidate has DSR 0.002-0.006 after ~14,000 trials.
- r2_lev2x's pre-registered 96-design grid has its pick failing the 1930-85 holdout (p 0.164). No design passing the hard filters gets a holdout p of 0.10 or lower.
- Averaged over start dates, p is 0.35 (2000-26) and 0.25 (1986-26), and the excess is +1.6 and +2.3, against the first-start +3.8 and +3.2.
- The website preset on real SSO (2006-26, CA) has p 0.116, a bootstrap CI that spans zero (about -1.0 to +7.8 pp/yr), and a Sharpe of 0.67 vs 0.65: the excess is leverage, not skill.
- The SMA175/3% parameter is the after-the-fact best point. SMA200/4% on the same real data gives +2.39, p 0.21 and a negative worst 10-year window.

(2) Endings. r2_gap4 shows that a CA investor who holds to a step-up or donates loses 0.7-1.1 pp/yr of the 2x edge. p doubles to 0.20-0.29, the worst 10-year window turns negative, and no 2x neighbourhood config passes items 1-3 in any history. A 20-year retirement sale also pushes p to 0.11-0.12. The engine's flat rates also ignore bracket creep from lumpy realizations, which only hurts the realizing strategy.

(3) Regime dependence. The edge comes entirely from slow bears: 2010s +0.6, 2020-26 -0.3, and for 2010-23 starts the SMA175 baseline averaged -0.47 to the end, negative in 47%. With 1-3 months of trend persistence the market-path bootstrap trails SPY in 57-66% of 20-year paths.

(4) Tails and mechanics:
- Execution must be at the same close: a one-day lag gives -59% in 1987 and p 0.26.
- One -20% day while invested costs about 40% of the account.
- 1929-32 still fell -77%.
- The market-path median DD is -59% to -66% vs SPY's -43% to -49%.
- SSO's financing and ordinary-income distributions, the IEF bond-bull dependence, and the near-zero-rate SSO era all make forward returns lower than in-sample.

(5) Behaviour. Pre-tax it trailed SPY in 13 of 26 calendar years, by 15-24 pp in five of them, and lost -37% to -41% in 2022 vs -24%. Those are the years investors abandon a rule, and they come before the rare payoff years.

(6) Momentum preset. Its expected edge is about zero (fails item 2, DSR 0.009, 1986+ twin negative). It carries uncompensated concentration and frozen-book risk (-56% to -71% in a replayed tech bust).

So buy-and-hold is the high-confidence answer to the question the user actually asked. The 2x trend is a legitimate but low-confidence, fat-tailed expected-value bet. It is best limited to a never-sold-core satellite, where drawdowns stay at or below SPY's but the whole-account benefit shrinks to about +0.3 to +0.6 pp/yr. 'High' confidence refers to the decision (nothing meets the bar, so default to buy-and-hold), not to buy-and-hold outperforming the 2x rule.

judge:1.pick: Buy and hold a low-cost S&P 500 index fund (VOO or IVV; SPY is equivalent) in the taxable account and do not sell it. No tested strategy beats it after California tax and costs with good confidence. The 2x trend preset is a leveraged bet with roughly +1 pp/yr expected and zero well inside its plausible range. It is not a confident way to beat the S&P.
caveats: **Nothing passed the bar.** No configuration passes the pre-registered 7-item 'good confidence' bar in California. After about 15,000-17,000 trials, the deflated Sharpe of every finalist is 0.002-0.06 against a 0.95 pass mark. Deflated against the 96-design round-2 grid alone, it is still only 0.28-0.54.

**Headline numbers are flattered.** They come from the first start date and the upper tail. January 2000 sat just before a slow bear market, the best possible start for a trend rule. Start-averaged p-values are 0.25-0.35. The 95 overlapping start dates contain only about 2-3 independent decades. The 100% ten-year beat rates are an artifact: 2008 or 2000-02 sits inside almost every window.

**The 1930-85 holdout is weak.** The trend rule is positive there but not significant (p 0.16-0.29), with a worst ten-year window of -5.8 to -7.4 pp/yr and drawdowns of -67% to -73%. It is not a clean holdout either: 200-day-average timing and 'leverage for the long run' became popular from exactly that 20th-century US record.

**It failed on other markets.** The same 2x rule on 33 other equity markets (2000-26, CA, each against its own buy-and-hold) had a median score of +0.24 and a pooled excess of -0.53 (p 0.60). Only 3% pass items 1-3. Even the Dow (DIA) shows -3.6 pp/yr against the S&P's +3.8. The trend filter reliably makes leverage less bad. Beating 1x also needs the market's return to clear borrowing costs and volatility drag, which the S&P did in 2009-26 and most markets did not.

**Its excess is leverage, not skill.** After-tax Sharpe is about the same as SPY's (0.67 vs 0.65 on real SSO; 0.64 vs 0.68 over 1986-2026). At SPY-like volatility (1.5x) the excess is +1.5 to +2.6 pp/yr and not significant (p 0.22-0.46). In effect it is a levered bet that US stocks keep outperforming their borrowing costs, and that trends last for months.

**The edge has faded since 2010.** All of the excess came from slow bear markets (1929-32, 1973-74, 2000-02, 2007-09): about 4 events in 96 years. Sixteen years with no slow bear cannot tell 'dormant' apart from 'gone'.

**The website setting is the luckiest neighbour.** SMA175 with a 3% band was carried over from an after-the-fact 3x pick. The pre-registered round-2 rule (SMA200, 3% band, with deferral) scores only +1.61 (p 0.21) on real tickers, and SMA200 with a 4% band on real SSO scores +2.39 (p 0.21).

**Holding until death or gifting changes the comparison.** If the shares end in a step-up or a gift, SPY's embedded 24.7% liquidation tax is forgiven. The 2x lead's California p then becomes 0.20-0.22, its worst ten-year window turns negative, and no 2x neighbour passes. Buy-and-hold's advantage over any strategy that realizes gains grows by about 0.8-0.9 pp/yr.

**Execution has to be exact.** Orders must go in market-on-close on the signal day. One day late, the 1986-2026 p rises to 0.26 and the drawdown reaches -59%, because the rule rides the 1987 crash. A single -20% day while at 2x removes about 40% of the account at that close.

**It loses more in fast drops.** In 2022 the preset fell -37% against the index's -25%. The pre-registered SMA200 version fell -38% vs -13% in 2015-16 and -36% vs -19% in 1998, and it trailed SPY in about half of calendar years (before tax), by 15-24 pp in the worst ones. Historical drawdowns run from -48% to -73%.

**Real-world tax and bond effects are not fully in the engine.** SSO pays ordinary-income distributions, as much as 4-5% of value in 2006-07. IEF interest is taxed every year. IEF added 1-1.4 pp/yr only because of the 1982-2020 bond bull market, and in 2022 both legs lost.

**The old momentum preset is not worth it.** 'Beat the S&P (CA)' has an expected edge of about 0. Its lead depends on QQQ and XLK being in the menu, and on rule-built menus (partial round-2 results) similar rules score -0.3 to +0.7. Its book freezes at 50-60% growth/tech: a replay of the 2000-02 tech bust on today's books loses -56% to -71%, against SPY's -47.5%.

**Some round-2 work is still running:** the futures overlay, valuation (CAPE), options overlays, specific-lot (HIFO) sales and the final rotation test. The futures overlay's early results look strong (never-sold 90% core plus a trend-gated futures overlay to 1.5x: p 0.001-0.02, drawdown about SPY's). But it was designed after the fact and is unverified, its Sharpe roughly equals SPY's (0.676 vs 0.683), its DSR is 0.01-0.12, it is not on the website, and it has no 1930-85 or cross-market check yet. A low p for a levered S&P position over a strong-return sample mostly confirms that stocks beat borrowing costs in that sample, not that the rule has skill.
**Research-only numbers.** The 2x history before 2006 is synthetic and 1930-85 uses a simulator, so those figures are research-only. The website can reproduce only the 2006+ real-SSO results.
**The preset's name overstates the evidence.** 'Beat the S&P: 2x trend (CA)' should be relabelled or carry a warning that it is a leveraged, low-confidence bet.

judge:1.reasoning:
I judged this as a statistical skeptic: how many configurations were tried, how much the winners are overfitted, what the holdouts say, how much depends on start date and era, and how much the edge has faded since 2010.

**(1) Search size.** Round 1 tried 13,778 configs, verification about 3,000 more variants, and round 2 several hundred more designs, roughly 15-17k trials in all. Every finalist's California DSR is 0.002-0.06 against a 0.95 pass mark, and nothing passes the pre-registered bar.

**(2) The 2x trend lead on the exact website config.** Real SSO/IEF, SMA175 with a 3% band, 2006-26 in CA: full-period excess +3.67, score +4.48, p 0.116. That already fails item 3 in-sample. SMA175/3% came from an after-the-fact 3x pick, and it is the top of 34 neighbours on 2000-26 (+5.3 against a median of about +3.2). The pre-registered round-2 pick scores only +1.61 (p 0.21) on real tickers. Choosing parameters inside the structure has no skill out of sample (PBO 0.47-0.82; walk-forward does no better than the average parameter set).

**(3) Start-date robustness.** The first-start p-values flatter the rule, because January 2000 sat just before a slow bear. Averaged over starts, p is 0.25-0.35 and excess to the end is +1.6 / +2.3. The 95 overlapping windows hold only about 2-3 independent decades.

**(4) Holdouts.** The 1930-85 holdout is positive (full-period excess +1.5 to +2.5) but not significant (p 0.16-0.29), and it is contaminated: 200-day-average timing became famous from that same US record. The cross-market test (r2_gap6, partial) is the most damaging new evidence. On 33 other equity markets, each against its own buy-and-hold, the median CA score is +0.24 and the pooled excess -0.53 (p 0.60); the Dow shows -3.6 against the S&P's +3.8. The decomposition shows what generalizes:
* the trend gate does rescue leverage from volatility drag (constant 2x scores -2.8, the trend-gated 2x +0.24);
* but beating 1x needs the market's return to clear borrowing costs, which the S&P did in 2009-26 and most markets did not.

**(5) Leverage, not skill.** After-tax Sharpe is about SPY's (0.67 vs 0.65; 0.64 vs 0.68 over 1986-2026). At SPY-like volatility the excess is not significant.

**(6) Fading since 2010.** Ten-year after-tax excess was +0.6 in the 2010s and -0.3 to -1.24 in 2020-26. SMA175 starts in 2010-23 average -0.47 to the end, and 47% of them are negative. The whole edge rests on about 4 slow bear markets in 96 years. With short trend persistence the rule trails SPY over 20 years in 57-66% of resampled paths.

**(7) How the position ends.** Under a step-up, the California p becomes 0.20-0.22, the worst ten-year window turns negative, and no 2x neighbour passes. Buy-and-hold's hurdle rises by about 0.8-0.9 pp/yr.

**(8) Execution.** With a one-day lag, the 1986-2026 p becomes 0.26 and the drawdown -59% (the 1987 crash).

**Net estimate.** Shrinking the in-sample +3.7 with all of the above gives about +1 pp/yr central, with zero well inside the plausible range and tracking error of about 13.5%/yr. That means roughly a 1-in-3 to 1-in-2 chance of trailing SPY over 20 years, which is not "good confidence".

**Momentum preset.** Score +0.66, fails the 10-year beat rate, DSR 0.009, random menus -0.13, rule-built menus about -0.3 to +0.7, negative before 2000 once distributions are taxed, -0.55 in 2010-20, plus frozen tech concentration. Its expected edge is about 0 with added risk.

**Futures overlay (preliminary).** The never-sold core plus a trend-gated futures overlay is the structurally right way to take the leverage bet in a taxable account: only the extra leverage is ever sold, it is taxed at the 60/40 blend, and tracking error is low, which explains its p of 0.001-0.02. But Sharpe roughly equals SPY's, DSR is 0.01-0.12, it was designed after the fact, it is unverified, it has no holdout or cross-market check, and the website cannot run it. It does not yet change the verdict.

**Conclusion.** For a California taxable account whose owner requires good confidence, buy and hold an S&P 500 fund and never sell. If the owner wants a deliberate bet, the only defensible form is a small leverage sleeve next to a never-sold core.

ranking: 1. Buy and hold an S&P 500 fund (VOO or IVV at 0.03% ER; SPY is fine) in the taxable account. Never sell. Harvest losses in a drawdown by swapping into a fund that tracks a different large-cap index (e.g. VOO to VV/SCHX).

2. Core-satellite: at least 80% VOO that is never sold, plus at most 20% in the site's 'Beat the S&P: 2x trend (CA)' rule, taken as an explicit bet. The sleeve belongs in an IRA/Roth if possible. The portfolio's excess is only about 20% of the sleeve's.
3. All-in 'Beat the S&P: 2x trend (CA)' preset: SSO while SPY is more than 3% above its 175-day SMA, IEF once it is more than 3% below, traded with market-on-close orders.

4. 'Beat the S&P (CA)' tax-managed momentum preset (TaxManagedCombo, 12-1 momentum, 1% gain budget): expected edge near 0, depends on QQQ/XLK being in the menu, and builds a growth/tech book that cannot be sold without a large tax bill.

5. r2_lev2x pre-registered pick S200|A2|IEF|D-h1 (SMA200/3% plus a 60-day short-term-gain defer): the site cannot express it, it is weaker on real tickers (2006+ CA score +1.61, p 0.21), and the defer can hold 2x through a crash.

6. r2_combos A3 (75% SPY never sold + 25% sleeve in a 3x fund on the trend rule, skimmed at exits): not on the site (no UPRO data, no core/sleeve skim), needs manual bookkeeping, and the 3x sleeve has severe tail risk.
7. 3x trend rules (UPRO SMA175/3% etc.): rejected for ruin-level tails (-88% to -93% in 1929-35).
judge:3.pick: Buy and hold an S&P 500 index fund (VOO or IVV; SPY is fine) in the California taxable account and realize as little as possible. Neither 'Beat the S&P' preset should be the main strategy. The 2x trend preset is at most a small, clearly labelled satellite bet, better placed in an IRA/Roth than in taxable.
judge:3.expected_excess_after_ca_tax:
**For the pick:** 0 pp/yr by construction. VOO/IVV add +0.03 to +0.04 over SPY on fees. Opportunistic loss harvesting is worth roughly +0.1 to +0.4 outside the engine, and only if the losses offset other gains or income.

**For the only serious alternative, the site's 2x trend preset run all-in:** an honest forward range is about -1 to +2.5 pp/yr.
- The central estimate is about +1 for an investor who sells within 10-20 years, and about 0 to +0.5 for one who would otherwise hold SPY to a step-up, donate it, or leave CA before selling.
- 1-sigma path noise over 20 years is about +/-3 pp/yr (tracking error about 13.5%/yr), so the odds of trailing SPY after 20 years are roughly 30-50%.

**Basis:**
- **The headline is one path.** The site's 2007-01 to 2026-07 window shows +3.63, and real SSO from 2006 shows full +3.67, score +4.48, p 0.116. That path is dominated by being in IEF from Nov 2007 to May 2009.
- **Start-averaged results are smaller.** The start-averaged to-the-end excess is +1.6 to +2.3. Starts from 2010-23 average -0.47 (47% negative) for this exact rule.
- **The site's own run since 2010 is about flat.** From 2010 its account grew 13.66%/yr after the taxes it paid, against SPY's 14.11% (step-up view). From 2020 it was 11.5% against 15.3%.
- **The holdout is weaker.** On 1930-85 the full excess is +1.5 and the score +2.95, with p 0.27.
- **A step-up costs about another 1 pp/yr.** For real SSO the score falls from +4.25 to +3.10 and p rises from 0.13 to 0.285.
- **Other markets did not repeat it.** On 33 other equity markets the same rule averaged -0.5 against their own buy-and-hold after CA tax (draft r2_gap6: median +0.24, 1 of 33 passes).
- **Flat 48.1/28.1 rates understate tax on lumpy realizations.** A six-figure exit pushes the federal long-term rate to 20% and CA into its 10.3-12.3% brackets. I estimate this unmodelled cost at about -0.2 to -0.6.
caveats: Nothing in roughly 13,800 round-1 configs plus thousands of verification and round-2 variants cleared the pre-registered good-confidence bar in CA. Buy-and-hold is the default because nothing beat it reliably, not because it was shown to win. Its expected excess is 0.

The 2x preset's +3.6 pp/yr after CA tax on the site is one 2007-2026 path, and its edge is the 2007-09 escape. Since 2010 the after-tax edge has been about zero: +0.7 to +1.5 on 10-year windows if you sell at the end, about -0.45/yr if you would otherwise hold SPY to a step-up, and negative over 2020-26. Run the preset on the site from 2010, 2015 and 2020 starts before trusting it.

The result moves a lot with the parameters on the same real-ticker data (2006-26, CA). SMA175/3% with no defer scores +4.48 (p 0.116), SMA200/4% +2.39 (p 0.21), and the pre-registered SMA200/3% with defer +1.61 (p 0.21). The deflated Sharpe is 0.002-0.006, and parameter selection inside the 2x structure has no skill before 1986 (PBO 0.60-0.82).

Cross-market check (r2_gap6, a draft, still running). The same 2x SMA175/3% rule on 33 other equity indexes averaged -0.53 pp/yr against each market's own buy-and-hold after CA tax (p 0.60). Only 1 of 33 passes items 1-3, and only 33% have a smaller drawdown than buy-and-hold. The S&P 500 is the outlier, so expect the edge to shrink.

Execution has to be exact. The signal includes today's close, so you need a market-on-close order entered around 3:45-3:50 pm ET (12:45 pm PT) on every signal day, based on a price estimate shortly before the close. The buy leg has to be sized from estimated sale proceeds, which needs a small cash buffer or a margin account. A one-day lag turned the 1987 escape into a -59% drawdown (1986-2026 p 0.26), and weekly checking fails. Check that your broker accepts MOC orders and their cutoff time.

Bracket stacking is not modelled; the site uses flat 48.1%/28.1% rates. In the site's own $100k-start run, one exit realized a $468k long-term gain (Feb 2022) and another a $135k short-term gain (Mar 2026). On top of $300k of wages, that puts the federal long-term rate at 20%, CA at 10.3-12.3%, and adds the 1% CA mental-health surcharge above $1M. The larger the account, the more the real tax exceeds the backtest's.

How the position ends matters. The site liquidates everything at the end, which charges SPY's deferred gain in full. If you would hold SPY until death, donate shares, or move out of California before selling, buy-and-hold's advantage grows by about 1 pp/yr against the 2x rule, and its p-value roughly doubles to 0.2-0.29.

Distributions are deferred inside the site's prices. In reality SSO pays non-qualified (ordinary) dividends, and IEF interest is taxed every year federally plus NIIT but is CA-exempt. Replays of the actual distribution history put the net effect at about -0.1 to 0 pp/yr in CA.

Wash sales are not enforced by the site. Re-entries within 30 days trigger them: in the site's run, IEF was sold at a $38.4k loss on 2022-03-29 and bought back on 2022-04-22. Cost is about 0.02-0.10 pp/yr. Turn off dividend reinvestment, and never buy SSO or IEF in an IRA or a spouse's account within 30 days of selling it at a loss.

The lab pick's 60-day short-term defer is dangerous in practice. On the site's path, the 2020-02-28 exit was 17 days short of long-term, and deferring it would have held 2x through most of the COVID crash (about -35%) to save about 2% of the position in tax.

Risk of the 2x rule: -48% drawdown (2006-26) up to -73% (1930s). Before tax it trailed SPY by 15-24 pp in 2011, 2015, 2016, 2020 and 2022, when it fell 37-41% against SPY's 24-25% and IEF also lost money. It needs slow, months-long bear markets to pay off. With only 1-3 months of trend persistence it trails SPY over 20 years 57-66% of the time. Higher T-bill rates also raise SSO's cost of leverage.

Lumpy realized gains mean large estimated-tax payments. Use the 110%-of-prior-year safe harbor to avoid underpayment penalties. Abandoning the rule after a bad year locks in the worst of it, and the realized tax cannot be undone.

Asset location: if the user wants the 2x trend bet, it belongs in an IRA/Roth, where real SSO scored +7.65 (p 0.016) untaxed, with VOO in the taxable account. Even untaxed, the cross-market evidence is weak (pooled +0.30, p 0.47).

Momentum preset: its expected edge is near 0. It depends on QQQ/XLK being in the menu (score -0.30 without them), fails the 10-year beat rate (70%), and freezes into a 50-60% growth/tech book with most of its value as unrealized gains.
judge:3.what_to_tell_the_user: About 14,000 strategy variations were tested, and none beat simply buying and holding an S&P 500 fund after California taxes with the confidence you asked for. For your taxable account, buy an S&P 500 index fund (VOO or IVV; SPY is fine), hold it, and sell as little as possible. The website's 'Beat the S&P: 2x trend (CA)' preset shows about +3.6 percentage points a year after tax from 2007 to 2026, but nearly all of that came from sidestepping the 2008 crash. Since 2010 its after-tax lead has been roughly zero, and since 2020 it has trailed. Most of its edge comes from leverage: it fell about 40% in 2022 when the S&P fell about 25%. It also only works if you trade at the market close on the exact day the signal fires, every time, for decades. Real taxes are worse than the site shows. One switch can realize a six-figure gain that pushes you into higher federal and California brackets. If you would otherwise hold the S&P fund until death, give shares to charity, or leave California before selling, buy-and-hold comes out further ahead. The same rule did no better than buy-and-hold on 33 other stock markets, which suggests the S&P result was partly luck. The older 'Beat the S&P (CA)' momentum preset has an expected edge near zero and drifts into a heavily growth/tech portfolio that you can't sell without a big tax bill. If you still want the leveraged bet, keep it to 10-20% of your money, ideally in an IRA or Roth where taxes don't eat it. Expect anything from losing 1 to gaining 2.5 points a year on that slice.
judge:3.reasoning:
From the implementation and tax lens, every friction the backtest leaves out works against the candidates, and the only one with a material edge, the 2x SSO/IEF trend rule, is already marginal inside the backtest (real SSO 2006+, CA: score +4.48, full +3.67, p 0.116; deflated Sharpe about 0.004).

**What I checked myself.**
- **The site preset matches the lab rule.** TrendSwitchTimer (SMA175/3%, daily, same close, SSO/IEF) is the lab rule, and its golden run reproduces +3.63 pp/yr after CA tax for 2007-2026.
- **The equity curves show where the edge came from.**
  - Jan 2007 to Jun 2009: +14.7 pp/yr.
  - 2010 to 2026: +4.45 pre-tax, but -0.45 after the taxes it actually paid, against SPY's untaxed deferral.
  - 2016 to 2026: -0.35.
  - 2020 to 2026: -3.8.
  - The lab's start-averaged figures agree: SMA175 starts from 2010-23 average -0.47, and 47% are negative.
  - So in a California taxable account the strategy amounts to a bet on slow, months-long bear markets, paid for by realizing leveraged gains at 28-48% plus whipsaw losses. With no such bear, the pre-tax leverage premium is taxed away.
- **Its trade log shows realism costs the engine does not model.**
  - Lumpy realizations: a $468k long-term gain in 2022 and a $135k short-term gain in 2026 on a $100k start. At $300k of wages these hit the 20% federal long-term rate and the 10.3-12.3% CA brackets, while the model uses flat 48.1/28.1.
  - A wash sale on the IEF re-entry in March/April 2022.
  - A same-close dependence that needs market-on-close discipline every signal day.

**Round-2 evidence.**
- **How the position ends.** Under a step-up or donation, real SSO's p goes to 0.285 and the score drops about 1.1 (r2_gap4).
- **Parameters.** On the same real tickers, SMA175/200 and the defer choice move the score between +1.6 and +4.5, so the headline point estimate is not reliable.
- **Other markets.** The draft r2_gap6 tables show the same rule on 33 other equity markets averaging -0.5 against their own buy-and-hold after CA tax. The 2000-2026 S&P 500 looks like the lucky member of the family.
- **Distributions and costs** are minor (about -0.1 to 0 and about -0.3 at 15 bps), so they do not rescue or sink it.

**The alternatives.**
- The r2_lev2x pick (SMA200 plus defer) cannot run on the site. On real tickers it is weaker (+1.61, p 0.21), and its defer can hold 2x through a crash (the Feb 2020 case on the site's path).
- The A3 core plus 3x sleeve needs UPRO and skim bookkeeping that the site lacks.
- The momentum preset is step-up-proof but its expected edge is about 0 and it depends on the menu.

**Why buy-and-hold.** It is the most tax-efficient holding in this engine. It gets stronger under a step-up, a donation or a move out of CA, needs no daily execution, and cannot be abandoned at the worst time. It is the only answer that meets 'good confidence'. The 2x trend is defensible only as a small, deliberate expected-value satellite, preferably in an IRA/Roth.
